# Introduction

## Intro

Reconstructing individual patient data (IPD) from published Kaplan–Meier (KM) survival curves has gradually become a common technical approach in secondary analysis and evidence synthesis in recent years [1–3]. When original IPD is unavailable due to privacy concerns, sharing costs, or data access limitations, researchers often have to rely on summary statistics reported in publications, such as median survival time or Cox hazard ratios; however, this summary information is usually insufficient to support more flexible or in-depth analytical needs, such as parametric survival model fitting and extrapolation, alternative effect measures in non-proportional hazards (non-PH) settings (e.g., RMST), subgroup and sensitivity analyses, and the construction of inputs for health economic models [1,2]. In this context, the iterative KM inversion algorithm proposed by Guyot et al. (often referred to as iterative KM, iKM, in subsequent literature) provides a practical framework for "approximately recovering original time-to-event data from KM curves" [1]. This framework typically relies on the digitization of the KM curve and, where possible, combines information on the number at risk and the number of events to construct pseudo-IPD consistent with the original curve by inverting the KM equation, thereby improving the feasibility and consistency of secondary analysis [1].

Although the iKM framework lays the methodological foundation, its practical application highly depends on the quality of the input data and the available information: researchers need to complete a series of steps, including curve coordinate extraction, axis label and scale identification, (if available) transcription of the number-at-risk table, and post-reconstruction verification; these steps are both time-consuming and prone to errors [2–4]. In the common use case of "not utilizing explicit censoring information (no censoring marks/no censoring time vector input)," existing mainstream tools show a clear consensus in their overall approach: they all center around iKM-like inversion, breaking down the problem into a pipeline of "curve digitization → data preprocessing → event/censoring allocation by interval → individual-level record generation → reconstructed curve verification"; meanwhile, the main improvements of different tools around iKM focus on three directions: firstly, improving the robustness of curve coordinate extraction and preprocessing, thereby reducing reconstruction deviations caused by pixel noise, non-monotonic points, and multi-curve interference; secondly, providing a more complete integrated workflow and visualization interface to lower the operational threshold from image to IPD and improve reproducibility; and thirdly, reducing manual transcription and parameter setting through automated or intelligent modules to improve batch processing efficiency [2–4].

However, compared to "only reconstructing consistent curve shapes," the handling of censoring is often one of the key factors affecting the credibility of reconstructed IPD and the stability of downstream inference [1,5]. Traditional iKM workflows, when lacking additional information, usually require simplified assumptions about the distribution of censoring within intervals (e.g., approximately uniform distribution), while the censoring mechanisms in real experiments may not satisfy such assumptions; more importantly, many KM plots in papers actually show censoring marks, but classic reconstruction processes do not directly utilize these "readable explicit censoring times" [5]. Therefore, the utilization and constraints of censoring information have become a clear direction for methodological improvements in recent years: some methods strengthen input extraction while maintaining the iKM framework (especially improving the quality of risk table and curve coordinate extraction), while others further incorporate "censoring time vectors marked on the graph" into the reconstruction constraints to reduce reliance on assumptions about interval censoring distribution and improve the accuracy of censoring structure reconstruction [4,5].

Based on the above methodological context, this paper focuses on three practical IPD reconstruction tools: IPDfromKM, KMtoIPD, and KM-GPT. All three are based on the iKM-like inversion framework, but they each have different emphases on "end-to-end workflow integration," "utilization of explicit censoring information," and "automated/intelligent input extraction" [2–5]. This paper aims to provide a comparative overview of these three tools, focusing on their input data requirements, core methods and assumptions, censoring handling strategies and limitations, and the operational workflow and reproducibility from KM plots to IPD output.  The paper is structured as follows: the methods section describes the tool selection and evaluation dimensions; the results section systematically summarizes the differences among the three tools and provides typical workflows and examples; and the discussion and conclusion section offers recommendations for tool selection based on different research objectives (e.g., methodological evaluation, evidence synthesis for systematic reviews, health economic modeling) and suggests directions for future improvements.

# R packages for IPD reconstruction from published Kaplan–Meier curves

## First paragraph: Intro

The primary focus of the study was on software designed to reconstruct individual patient data (IPD) from published Kaplan–Meier (KM) curves for time-to-event analyses. Although the common workflow for digitising KM curves involves the use of image-extraction tools and reconstruction in Stata, this approach can be cumbersome and less convenient for downstream analyses. Consequently, the focus was directed towards integrated solutions implemented in R.

In this context, three IPD reconstruction tools were selected that signify substantive advances over earlier iKM-based implementations: IPDfromKM, KMtoIPD, and KM-GPT. KMtoIPD emphasizes more explicit handling of truncation times and uses a richer set of reconstruction parameters; IPDfromKM provides an end-to-end workflow via an R/Shiny interface, enabling KM digitization, preprocessing, and IPD reconstruction within a single environment; and KM-GPT leverages AI-assisted extraction to improve the quality of inputs supplied to iKM-style reconstruction. The following sections describe the overall framework of these three tools, with a focus on required inputs, core methodology, and practical workflows from KM curve images to reconstructed IPD. Detailed information on data specifications, modeling assumptions, and implementation details can be found in the corresponding manuals and primary publications for each tool.

## Main Feature (Table 2)

Table 2 summarizes the availability of reconstruction-related features across the three IPD reconstruction tools (KMtoIPD, IPDfromKM, and KM-GPT). Although all three aim to reconstruct time-to-event IPD from published Kaplan–Meier curves, they differ in how they operationalize the iKM-style reconstruction workflow and, critically, in what auxiliary information they can exploit to constrain the reconstruction. In particular, features related to risk-table utilization and censoring handling are key considerations because they directly determine how well the reconstructed IPD can reproduce not only the published survival curve but also the underlying event/censoring structure.
With respect to risk tables, IPDfromKM and KM-GPT explicitly leverage number-at-risk information, whereas KMtoIPD does not. For IPDfromKM, the risk table is incorporated through an interval-based preprocessing step (via preprocess()), which enforces monotonicity and applies interval-level constraints consistent with the reported numbers at risk. KM-GPT similarly uses risk-table information, but differs by attempting to automatically extract the risk table from the published figure and then imposing interval constraints within its pipeline. In contrast, KMtoIPD primarily relies on the digitized KM curve (and, when available, user-supplied censoring information), meaning that risk-table–based calibration and robustness checks are limited. Consistent with this, the table indicates that IPDfromKM and KM-GPT offer more explicit pathways to calibrate reconstructions back to paper-reported quantities (e.g., total events or checks against numbers at risk), and they are better positioned to recover from risk-table errors via manual adjustment (IPDfromKM) or pipeline-supported iterative handling (KM-GPT), whereas KMtoIPD lacks a comparable built-in mechanism.
Regarding censoring, Table 2 highlights that both KMtoIPD and IPDfromKM can generate reconstructed datasets that include censoring and can accommodate censoring ties (multiple censorings at identical time points), but KM-GPT does not clearly specify comparable event-versus-censor assignment behavior at the reconstruction stage in the current description. The tools also differ in how censoring information is obtained and allocated. KMtoIPD depends on external digitization or user-supplied censoring times; accordingly, it has limited support for censoring-mark extraction when marks are occluded or overlapping. IPDfromKM likewise does not target automated extraction of censoring marks, typically relying on manual/interactive workflows. By contrast, KM-GPT is designed to cope with noisy figures and overlapping graphical elements at the extraction stage, which may improve performance when censoring marks are difficult to read. Once censoring times are not explicitly available, within-interval censoring allocation becomes a modeling choice: KMtoIPD relies on user-supplied censoring times or conventional assumptions, while IPDfromKM typically uses a default allocation rule within intervals (often effectively uniform), and KM-GPT is described as using a more adaptive or uncertainty-aware strategy (implementation-specific). All three approaches implicitly or explicitly handle administrative censoring through the maximum follow-up time, with KM-GPT indicating more explicit handling in its pipeline.
Finally, Table 2 contrasts reconstruction mechanics and assumptions that affect robustness and reproducibility. All three support monotonicity correction for non-monotone digitized curves (either directly or via preprocessing settings). However, KM-GPT is distinct in offering features that are largely absent in the other two tools, including support for log-scaled time axes and stochastic reconstruction with reproducibility controls (e.g., random seeds). These differences reflect broader trade-offs in tool design: KMtoIPD emphasizes parameterized reconstruction using user-supplied censoring times; IPDfromKM emphasizes an integrated, user-facing workflow with explicit preprocessing and calibration hooks; and KM-GPT emphasizes automation of extraction and additional flexibility in handling challenging figures and specialized axis scaling.

## Package Intro (guidebook)

The KMtoIPD package provides a focused set of tools to reconstruct individual patient data (IPD) from published Kaplan–Meier (KM) survival curves by explicitly incorporating censoring times marked on the KM plot, following the method proposed by Rogula et al. (2022). The underlying algorithm was developed to address a common limitation of earlier KM-reconstruction approaches—namely, that exact censoring times are often visually available on published KM curves but are not used—and instead incorporates these censoring times into the reconstructed IPD “exactly as specified” when they can be extracted. In practice, KMtoIPD takes as inputs the total sample size, the digitized coordinates of survival drops, and the digitized censoring times, and returns a patient-level dataset (survival time plus event indicator) suitable for downstream survival modeling. In the original methodological evaluation, Rogula et al. assessed reliability via simulation (simulate → digitize → reconstruct), comparing hazard ratios and survival quantiles between original and reconstructed data and visually inspecting reconstructed curves, and reported no systematic differences and close curve fit. The method is particularly appropriate when censoring marks are clearly distinguishable, because performance depends on the quality of extracted censoring times.
